title: Executive Leadership Intensive
blurb: Three days onsite for directors and VPs, followed by 90 days of executive coaching. Strategy, influence, and leading leaders in the AI era.

modules.t: Day 1A — Strategy: Diagnosis, Choices & Coherent Action
modules.d: What strategy actually is, how to recognise bad strategy, and how to articulate yours in one page.
modules.body:
Most "strategies" are not strategies

Executives are surrounded by documents called strategy that are really goals, slogans, budgets or lists of initiatives. Richard Rumelt, in Good Strategy / Bad Strategy, identifies the hallmarks of bad strategy: fluff (impressive language with little meaning), failure to face the challenge (no clear diagnosis of what is hard), mistaking goals for strategy ("grow revenue 20%" is a desire, not a way), and bad strategic objectives (long lists of unprioritised initiatives). A strategy that does not tell people what not to do is not doing its job.

The kernel of good strategy

Rumelt's kernel has three parts. A diagnosis names the critical challenge — what makes this situation difficult and where the leverage lies. A guiding policy is the overall approach to overcoming that challenge, ruling out many options. Coherent actions are coordinated steps — resource commitments, policies, initiatives — that reinforce one another to carry out the guiding policy. The diagnosis is usually where executives under-invest: if the challenge is wrongly framed, excellent execution solves the wrong problem.

Example. A regional training institute faces declining enrolment. Goal-as-strategy: "Increase enrolment 30%." Kernel: Diagnosis — employers no longer value our generic certificates; graduates cannot show applied skill. Guiding policy — become the provider whose graduates demonstrably do the work, by partnering with employers on applied, assessed programmes. Coherent actions — co-design three programmes with employers; replace written exams with portfolio assessment; retire five low-demand courses to fund the redesign; publish placement outcomes.

Strategy as a set of choices

A. G. Lafley and Roger Martin's Playing to Win frames strategy as five integrated choices: What is our winning aspiration? Where will we play? How will we win? What capabilities must be in place? What management systems are required? "Where to play" and "how to win" are the heart: which customers, geographies, channels and offerings, and what distinctive advantage — cost leadership or differentiation — will make you win there. Choices must be mutually reinforcing; an aspiration to be premium with a cost-cutting capability system will fail.

Analysing the environment without drowning in it

Executives use frameworks to sharpen the diagnosis, not to fill slides. PESTLE scans political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental forces. Porter's five forces examines industry attractiveness: rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, buyer power and supplier power. Capability analysis asks which of your resources are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and organised to exploit (the VRIO test). The insight comes from asking "So what does this mean for our choices?" after each analysis.

Portfolio prioritisation

Most organisations attempt too many initiatives at once, starving each of the attention and talent it needs. Executive prioritisation involves explicitly ranking initiatives against strategic fit, value, risk and capacity, then stopping lower-ranked ones — the hardest and most valuable leadership act. A useful discipline: no new strategic initiative is approved without naming what will be stopped or slowed to make room.

Articulating strategy so people can act on it

If managers two levels below you cannot explain the strategy and how their work fits, it does not exist in practice. A one-page strategy should state the aspiration, the diagnosis, the where-to-play and how-to-win choices, the three to five priority actions, what you will stop, and the measures of progress. Then repeat it — leaders consistently underestimate how often strategy must be communicated before it is understood and used.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my strategy sparring partner. I will describe my organisation's situation. First, push me for a sharper diagnosis of the critical challenge. Then help me write Rumelt's kernel (diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions) and the five Playing to Win choices. Finally, identify which current initiatives contradict the strategy and should be stopped, and draft a one-page strategy.

📚 Glossary

  • Kernel: diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent actions
  • Bad strategy: fluff, unfaced challenges, goals posing as strategy, or unprioritised objectives
  • Where to play / how to win: the core strategic choices of arena and advantage
  • VRIO: valuable, rare, inimitable, organised — tests for sustained advantage
  • Portfolio prioritisation: ranking and stopping initiatives to focus capacity

📖 References

  • Rumelt, R. (2011). Good Strategy / Bad Strategy.
  • Lafley, A. G. & Martin, R. (2013). Playing to Win.
  • Porter, M. (1979/2008). The five competitive forces that shape strategy. Harvard Business Review.
  • Barney, J. (1991). Firm resources and sustained competitive advantage. Journal of Management.

quiz.q: A board approves a 'strategy' that reads: 'Become the region's leading provider, grow revenue 25% and delight customers.' What is the MOST significant weakness?
opts: It states goals without diagnosing the challenge or choosing how to win
It is too short to be credible
It lacks a mission statement
The revenue target is too ambitious
quiz.x: These are aspirations. Without a diagnosis and guiding policy, the document does not guide choices.

quiz.q: In Rumelt's kernel, which element is MOST often neglected and causes excellent execution of the wrong plan?
opts: Coherent actions
Diagnosis
Budget allocation
Communication
quiz.x: If the critical challenge is misframed, even well-coordinated actions solve the wrong problem.

quiz.q: A company aims to be the premium, high-service brand while its operating model is built around minimising headcount in customer support. What does Playing to Win identify as the problem?
opts: The winning aspiration is too vague
Where to play is too broad
The management systems are too complex
The choices are not mutually reinforcing
quiz.x: Strategic choices must reinforce each other; a premium positioning needs capabilities that support high service.

quiz.q: An executive team agrees on 14 strategic priorities for the year. What is the MOST likely result?
opts: Higher engagement because everyone has a priority
Better risk diversification
Attention and talent spread too thin, with few priorities achieved well
Faster growth through broad coverage
quiz.x: Too many priorities starve each of focus. Strategy requires saying no.

quiz.q: Which rule BEST enforces disciplined portfolio prioritisation?
opts: No new strategic initiative is approved without naming what will be stopped or slowed
Review the portfolio only every three years
Let each department choose its own priorities
Approve every initiative with a positive business case
quiz.x: Tying new commitments to stopping others forces real trade-offs.

quiz.q: A Porter's five forces analysis shows strong buyer power and many substitutes. What is the MOST useful next step?
opts: Increase prices to offset buyer power
Repeat the analysis with a different framework
Present the analysis to the board as is
Ask what these forces imply for where to play and how to win
quiz.x: Analysis is valuable only when translated into implications for strategic choices.

quiz.q: A firm's key capability is valuable and rare, but competitors could copy it within a year. Under VRIO, what does this suggest?
opts: A sustained competitive advantage
A temporary competitive advantage
No competitive advantage
A competitive disadvantage
quiz.x: Valuable and rare but imitable resources give a temporary advantage; sustained advantage requires inimitability and organisation.

quiz.q: Middle managers cannot explain how their work connects to the strategy, though it was presented at an annual conference. What is the BEST executive response?
opts: Hire a consultant to explain it
Replace managers who do not understand it
Create a one-page strategy and communicate it repeatedly through regular conversations
Require managers to reread the strategy document
quiz.x: Strategy must be simple and repeated far more often than leaders expect before people can act on it.

quiz.q: Which statement is the BEST example of a guiding policy?
opts: Launch a new website
Increase market share to 40%
Win by becoming the provider whose graduates demonstrably perform on the job, through employer co-designed programmes
Hire 50 new staff
quiz.x: A guiding policy sets the approach to overcome the diagnosed challenge and rules out alternatives; the others are goals or actions.

quiz.q: An executive argues that 'our strategy is to be flexible and do whatever the market wants'. What is the strategic weakness?
opts: Flexibility is never valuable
It makes no choices about where to play or how to win, so it cannot guide resource allocation
It is too specific
It ignores the five forces
quiz.x: A strategy that excludes nothing provides no guidance for decisions or resource commitments.

modules.d: Making high-stakes decisions under uncertainty, defeating bias, and using AI as a challenger.
modules.body:
Judge decisions by their quality, not just their outcomes

Annie Duke calls the habit of judging decisions by their results "resulting". Good decisions sometimes lead to bad outcomes because of luck; bad decisions sometimes lead to good ones. Executives who evaluate only outcomes learn the wrong lessons — punishing sound bets that were unlucky and rewarding reckless ones that worked. Decision quality asks: Was the frame right? Were real alternatives considered? Was relevant information sought at reasonable cost? Were values and trade-offs explicit? Was the reasoning sound? Was there commitment to action?

One-way and two-way doors

Jeff Bezos distinguished Type 1 decisions — consequential and hard to reverse, "one-way doors" — from Type 2 decisions — reversible "two-way doors". Type 1 decisions deserve deliberation, broad input and careful analysis. Type 2 decisions should be made quickly by small groups or individuals, because the cost of delay exceeds the cost of a reversible mistake. A common executive failure is applying heavy Type 1 process to every decision, which slows the organisation and centralises decisions that should be delegated.

The biases that distort executive judgement

  • Confirmation bias — seeking evidence that supports the preferred option.
  • Overconfidence — estimate ranges that are far too narrow; plans assume best cases.
  • Planning fallacy — systematically underestimating time and cost.
  • Sunk-cost fallacy — continuing because of what has already been invested.
  • Anchoring — over-relying on the first number heard.
  • Groupthink — cohesive teams suppressing dissent to maintain harmony.
  • Escalation of commitment — doubling down on a failing course to justify past choices.

Knowing about biases does little to reduce them individually; what works is process that builds in correction.

Process tools that improve decisions

The pre-mortem (Gary Klein): imagine it is a year from now and the decision has failed badly; each person writes down why. This legitimises dissent and surfaces risks that optimism hides. The outside view / reference-class forecasting (Kahneman and Flyvbjerg): instead of building estimates from your own plan, start with the actual outcomes of similar projects — how long and how much they really took — then adjust. Devil's advocate and red teams: assign someone explicitly to attack the preferred option. Multiple options: insisting on at least three genuine alternatives reduces narrow framing ("whether or not" decisions). Decision journals: record the reasoning, expectations and confidence at the time, so later review evaluates the decision, not the luck.

Expected value and scenarios. For major choices, build three to four plausible futures and estimate outcomes under each. Ask which option performs acceptably across all scenarios (robustness), not only which is best in the most likely one. Expected value helps, but for Type 1 decisions also ask: can we survive the worst case?

Using AI as a challenger, not an oracle

Generative AI is a powerful decision aid when used as a challenger: generating alternatives you missed, arguing the opposing case, running structured scenario analysis, drafting the pre-mortem, or stress-testing assumptions. Its risks are real: plausible but false facts, sycophancy toward the framing you give it, and hidden assumptions. Good practice: ask it explicitly to argue against your preferred option, verify every factual claim that matters, and keep accountability human. Never let a fluent answer substitute for evidence.

Who decides: decision rights

Many executive decision problems are really unclear decision rights. Frameworks such as RAPID (Recommend, Agree, Perform, Input, Decide) or a RACI matrix clarify who decides, who must agree, and who provides input. Ambiguity produces either paralysis or conflict; clarity allows speed.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my executive decision red team. My decision: [describe]. Step 1: classify it as a one-way or two-way door and say what process it deserves. Step 2: generate at least two genuine alternatives I have not considered. Step 3: run a pre-mortem listing the five most likely reasons it fails. Step 4: give me an outside-view base rate from similar decisions. Step 5: argue forcefully against my preferred option. Flag any facts I must verify.

📚 Glossary

  • Resulting: judging a decision by its outcome rather than its quality
  • One-way / two-way door: irreversible versus reversible decisions
  • Pre-mortem: imagining failure in advance to surface risks
  • Reference-class forecasting: estimating from outcomes of similar past cases
  • RAPID: framework clarifying decision roles

📖 References

  • Duke, A. (2018). Thinking in Bets.
  • Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, Fast and Slow.
  • Klein, G. (2007). Performing a project premortem. Harvard Business Review.
  • Flyvbjerg, B. & Gardner, D. (2023). How Big Things Get Done.
  • Bezos, J. (2016). Letter to Amazon shareholders.
  • Rogers, P. & Blenko, M. (2006). Who has the D? Harvard Business Review.

quiz.q: A CEO approved an acquisition after thorough diligence, multiple options and explicit risk analysis. An unforeseeable regulatory change then made it unprofitable. The board wants to remove the CEO for a 'bad decision'. What does decision-quality thinking suggest?
opts: The decision was bad because it was irreversible
The CEO should have avoided all acquisitions
The board is right, since the outcome was poor
The board may be 'resulting' — judging by outcome rather than the quality of the decision process
quiz.x: A sound process can produce a bad outcome through luck. Evaluate the decision on frame, alternatives, information and reasoning.

quiz.q: An executive committee spends three meetings deciding which project-management software to pilot for one team. What is the MOST likely error?
opts: Applying one-way-door process to a reversible two-way-door decision
Insufficient analysis for a strategic decision
Anchoring
Groupthink
quiz.x: Reversible, low-consequence decisions should be made quickly and close to the work.

quiz.q: A project leadership team is highly confident in a new launch. Which tool BEST surfaces hidden risks while legitimising dissent?
opts: A satisfaction survey
A pre-mortem imagining the launch has failed
A SWOT analysis
A vote on whether to proceed
quiz.x: The pre-mortem makes it safe and expected to name reasons for failure that optimism hides.

quiz.q: A ministry estimates a new IT system will take 18 months, based on its detailed project plan. Similar government systems have typically taken 36–48 months. What should the executive do?
opts: Trust the detailed plan, which is specific to this project
Shorten the plan to 12 months to create urgency
Use the outside view: start from the reference-class outcomes and adjust, revising the estimate upward
Average the two figures
quiz.x: Reference-class forecasting counters the planning fallacy by anchoring on what similar projects actually took.

quiz.q: A company has spent $40 million on a product line that analysis now shows will never be profitable. Executives argue for another $10 million 'so we don't waste the investment'. Which biases are MOST evident?
opts: Planning fallacy and availability
Anchoring and confirmation bias
Overconfidence and groupthink
Sunk-cost fallacy and escalation of commitment
quiz.x: Past investment is irrelevant to future value; continuing to justify it is escalation of commitment.

quiz.q: An executive asks an AI assistant, 'Explain why our expansion into Ghana is a strong move.' What is the MOST significant limitation of this use?
opts: The framing invites the AI to confirm the preferred option rather than challenge it
AI cannot analyse markets
The question is too specific
AI responses are always too long
quiz.x: AI tends to follow the framing given. Asking it to argue against the option and verifying facts turns it into a challenger.

quiz.q: A leadership team is choosing between 'launch now' and 'don't launch'. What is the BEST way to improve this decision?
opts: Generate at least one or two genuine additional alternatives
Gather more data on the launch option only
Delay until the market is certain
Ask the most senior person to decide
quiz.x: 'Whether or not' framing is a common trap; real alternatives (phased launch, pilot, partner) often improve outcomes.

quiz.q: Two divisions keep fighting over who has final say on pricing, delaying launches. What is the MOST likely root problem?
opts: Poor market analysis
Unclear decision rights
Lack of AI tools
Insufficient data
quiz.x: Repeated conflict and delay often reflect ambiguity over who decides; frameworks such as RAPID clarify roles.

quiz.q: A strategy performs best in the most likely scenario but would bankrupt the company in a plausible downturn. Another performs adequately in all scenarios. For a one-way-door decision, which consideration is MOST important?
opts: Ignore the downturn because it is unlikely
Choose the highest expected value regardless of downside
Consider robustness and survivability across scenarios, not only the most likely case
Choose whichever the CEO prefers
quiz.x: For irreversible decisions, the ability to survive the worst plausible case can matter more than maximising the likely case.

quiz.q: Why does the course recommend keeping a decision journal?
opts: To replace board minutes
To provide legal protection
To share decisions on social media
To record reasoning and confidence at the time, so later reviews evaluate the decision rather than the luck
quiz.x: Hindsight rewrites memory; contemporaneous records allow honest learning.

modules.t: Day 2 — Influence, Executive Communication & Leading Leaders
modules.d: Influencing without authority, communicating to boards, and building the leadership bench beneath you.
modules.body:
Influence at the top is mostly lateral and upward

Senior leaders discover that formal authority matters less as they rise. Peers run their own divisions, boards hold ultimate authority, partners and regulators are outside the hierarchy. Executive effectiveness depends on influence without authority: building agreement among people who do not have to agree with you.

The currencies of influence

Allan Cohen and David Bradford's model treats influence as exchange: understand what the other person values — their "currencies" — and what you can offer. Currencies include resources, information, visibility, support for their goals, recognition, relationship, and alignment with their values or mission. Influence fails when executives offer only what they value. Robert Cialdini's research identifies durable principles of persuasion — reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity and unity (shared identity). Used ethically, they help good ideas get heard; used manipulatively, they destroy trust once discovered.

Stakeholder mapping at the executive level

Before any major initiative, map the stakeholders whose support or resistance will decide it: their interests, influence, current position, and what would move them. Meet the most influential sceptics before the decision meeting. Executive decisions are rarely made in the meeting; they are made in the conversations beforehand. A proposal that surprises key stakeholders in a board meeting usually fails.

Communicating to boards and senior audiences

Boards and executive committees have limited time and broad responsibilities. Barbara Minto's pyramid principle structures communication for them: lead with the answer or recommendation, then the key supporting arguments, then the supporting data. This reverses the academic habit of building up to a conclusion. A strong board paper states what decision is needed, the recommendation, the reasons, the risks and mitigations, the alternatives considered, and what success will look like — ideally on one or two pages, with detail in appendices.

Data storytelling. Executives need insight, not data dumps. One chart that shows the critical trend, clearly labelled, with a headline stating the conclusion ("Applications from employer partners have tripled since 2024") is worth more than ten tables. Pair numbers with a concrete example that makes them human.

Leading leaders: the pipeline transitions

Ram Charan, Stephen Drotter and James Noel's Leadership Pipeline describes the transitions leaders must make as they rise: from managing self to managing others, to managing managers, to managing a function, to a business, to a group, to an enterprise. At each transition, leaders must change three things: skills, time application and work values — what they believe is important work. The most common failure: a senior leader who still values the work they used to do, and so micromanages managers and starves strategic work of time.

Leading managers means developing their leadership, not doing their jobs: selecting and developing first-line leaders, holding them accountable for leading (not just producing), coaching them through their own transitions, and building cross-team collaboration.

Building the bench: succession and development

An executive's legacy is measured partly by the strength of the leaders they leave behind. Practical steps: identify critical roles and potential successors; distinguish readiness now from potential; give high-potential leaders stretch assignments with support; use the 70-20-10 guide (most development comes from challenging experience, some from relationships and feedback, a smaller part from formal learning); and review the bench regularly with the same seriousness as financial results.

Managing up and working with boards

Effective executives understand their board's or superior's priorities, pressures and preferred communication style; raise problems early with options; never let them be surprised by bad news from someone else; and respect the boundary between governance (board) and management (executive). Disagreements are voiced clearly in private and decisions, once made, are supported in public — unless they cross an ethical line.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my board communication coach. I will paste a draft board paper or describe a proposal. Rewrite it using the pyramid principle: decision required, recommendation, three key reasons, risks and mitigations, alternatives considered, success measures — within one page. Then role-play the two most sceptical board members, asking the hardest questions, and evaluate my answers.

📚 Glossary

  • Influence without authority: gaining agreement from people outside your control
  • Currencies: what stakeholders value and can be exchanged
  • Pyramid principle: communicate the answer first, then supporting logic
  • Leadership pipeline: the series of leadership transitions requiring new skills, time use and values
  • 70-20-10: development mostly through experience, then relationships, then formal learning

📖 References

  • Cohen, A. & Bradford, D. Influence Without Authority.
  • Cialdini, R. (2021). Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion (new and expanded).
  • Minto, B. The Pyramid Principle.
  • Charan, R., Drotter, S. & Noel, J. (2011). The Leadership Pipeline.
  • Center for Creative Leadership — 70-20-10 framework.

quiz.q: A COO needs support from the head of sales, who sees no benefit in a new operations system. Which approach BEST applies the currencies model?
opts: Explain how efficient the system is for operations
Identify what the head of sales values — e.g. faster order-to-delivery for key clients — and show how the system serves it
Ask the CEO to instruct the head of sales
Offer to delay the project until sales is ready
quiz.x: Influence works through what the other party values. Leading with your own benefits or escalating rarely builds commitment.

quiz.q: An executive plans to present a major restructuring for the first time at the board meeting, to 'see their reactions'. What is the MOST significant risk?
opts: Key stakeholders are surprised and resist, since decisions are often shaped in prior conversations
The restructuring will be leaked
The presentation will be too long
The board will approve it too quickly
quiz.x: Engaging influential stakeholders beforehand allows concerns to be addressed; surprises tend to produce defensiveness.

quiz.q: Which board paper opening BEST follows the pyramid principle?
opts: The following data tables summarise office performance
Background: In 2019, the organisation began reviewing its regional structure…
We recommend consolidating three regional offices into one hub, saving $1.2M annually with minimal service impact, for decision today.
This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of several options
quiz.x: Lead with the decision and recommendation; supporting reasons and data follow.

quiz.q: A newly promoted director of a 300-person function still personally reviews every report his former team produces. According to the leadership pipeline, what has he failed to change?
opts: His technical knowledge
His job title
Only his skills
His work values and time application — he still values his former work
quiz.x: Transitions require valuing new kinds of work. Holding onto old work starves strategic responsibilities and disempowers managers.

quiz.q: An executive includes 14 detailed tables in a board update to show thoroughness. What would MOST improve its impact?
opts: Adding more tables for completeness
Removing all data
Reading the tables aloud in the meeting
One or two clearly labelled charts with headline conclusions, with detail in an appendix
quiz.x: Boards need insight; data storytelling highlights the critical trend and conclusion.

quiz.q: A CEO disagrees privately with a board decision that is legal and ethical but, in her view, unwise. After voicing concerns, the board confirms the decision. What should she do?
opts: Delay implementation until the board changes its mind
Tell staff she disagrees with the board
Support and implement the decision publicly, while continuing to monitor and report on outcomes
Resign immediately
quiz.x: Disagree privately, then commit publicly — unless an ethical line is crossed — while keeping the board informed.

quiz.q: Which development plan for a high-potential manager is MOST consistent with 70-20-10?
opts: Enrol them in three leadership courses
Give them a stretch assignment leading a cross-functional project, with a mentor and regular feedback, plus a targeted course
Ask them to read leadership books
Wait until a promotion opens
quiz.x: Development comes mostly from challenging experience, supported by relationships and some formal learning.

quiz.q: A persuasive executive uses false scarcity ('this offer ends tonight') to push partners into a decision. What is the MOST serious risk?
opts: Influence based on manipulation damages trust once discovered
The partners may decide too slowly
It violates the pyramid principle
Scarcity never influences anyone
quiz.x: Persuasion principles must be used truthfully. Manipulation produces short-term compliance and long-term distrust.

quiz.q: In succession planning, why distinguish 'readiness now' from 'potential'?
opts: Potential matters only for junior roles
Someone may have high potential but need development before taking a role, which shapes the development plan
Readiness is measured by tenure
They mean the same thing
quiz.x: Separating the two prevents both premature promotions and overlooking future leaders, and targets development.

quiz.q: A senior leader learns of a major project failure that will affect the CEO's commitments to the board. What should she do?
opts: Report it in the quarterly review
Let the project manager inform the CEO
Wait until she has fixed it to avoid alarming the CEO
Inform the CEO promptly with the facts, impact and options
quiz.x: Managing up means no surprises: raise significant problems early, with options.

modules.d: Redesigning operating models, governing AI responsibly, and leading change at scale.
modules.body:
Transformation is not a bigger project

A transformation changes how the organisation creates value — its operating model, culture and capabilities — not just a system or a structure. Research and practitioner surveys have repeatedly found that most large transformations fall short of their goals, usually not because the design was wrong, but because leaders underestimated the human, cultural and capability work. Executives who treat transformation as a technical programme managed by a project office tend to fail; those who lead it personally and visibly tend to succeed.

The operating model

An operating model describes how the organisation delivers its strategy: processes (how work flows), organisation (structure, roles, decision rights), people (capabilities, culture, incentives), technology and data, location, and governance and performance management. Redesign starts from the strategy's "how to win" choices and asks which capabilities must be strengthened, which are no longer needed, and how the parts must change together. Changing structure alone — the most common executive move — rarely changes performance, because processes, incentives and behaviours stay the same.

Leading change at scale

John Kotter's eight steps remain a practical checklist: create a sense of urgency grounded in real data; build a guiding coalition of credible leaders; form a clear vision and strategy; communicate it far more than seems necessary; remove obstacles — including leaders who resist; generate short-term wins that prove the change works; sustain acceleration without declaring victory too soon; and anchor the change in culture through promotion, hiring and stories. Kotter's research found that skipping steps creates an illusion of speed and rarely produces results.

The productivity J-curve. Major technology adoption often makes performance worse before it gets better: people learn new tools, processes are redesigned and old habits persist. Executives who expect immediate gains often abandon transformations in the dip. Planning for the J-curve — budgeting time, setting realistic milestones and communicating the expected dip — protects the investment.

The business case for AI adoption

A credible AI business case identifies specific use cases tied to strategic priorities, the expected value (time saved, quality improved, revenue created, risk reduced), the full costs (licences, integration, data preparation, training, change management, governance), the risks, and the measures that will show value. The strongest early cases are usually narrow, high-volume and measurable — document processing, customer response drafting, data analysis — rather than broad promises of transformation. Pilots should have clear success criteria and a decision point: scale, adjust or stop.

Executive AI governance

AI governance makes adoption safe and trustworthy. Executives own its foundations: a clear policy for acceptable use; accountability — named owners for each AI system; risk assessment proportional to impact (an AI that drafts internal summaries needs less control than one that influences hiring, credit or medical decisions); data protection and privacy; human oversight for consequential decisions; testing and monitoring for accuracy, bias and drift; transparency with users and clients; and incident response. Recognised frameworks — the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) and the ISO/IEC 42001 AI management system standard — provide structure, and regulations such as the EU AI Act classify systems by risk level. Executives in Africa should also follow national data protection laws and emerging continental guidance.

Culture: the decisive factor

Culture is the pattern of behaviour that is rewarded and tolerated. Executives shape it less through statements than through what they pay attention to, how they react to crises, what they role-model, how they allocate resources, and whom they promote and remove — Edgar Schein's "primary embedding mechanisms". A transformation that preaches experimentation but punishes failure, or promotes leaders who block change, teaches the opposite of its message.

Your personal transformation charter

You leave Day 3 with a one-page charter: the transformation's purpose and diagnosis, the target operating-model changes, the first three short-term wins, the guiding coalition, the AI use cases and governance safeguards, the key risks, the measures of success, and your personal role — what you will do, stop doing and model differently. This charter becomes the agenda for your 90-day coaching sprint.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my transformation architect. I will describe my organisation and the change I need. Help me diagnose the operating-model elements that must change together, map my change plan to Kotter's eight steps, identify three AI use cases with value, cost, risk and governance safeguards, anticipate the J-curve, and draft a one-page personal transformation charter including what I personally must start, stop and model.

📚 Glossary

  • Operating model: how processes, organisation, people, technology, location and governance deliver strategy
  • Guiding coalition: credible leaders who drive the change together
  • J-curve: temporary performance dip during major adoption
  • AI governance: policies, accountability and controls for responsible AI use
  • NIST AI RMF: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage framework for AI risk
  • Embedding mechanisms: leader behaviours that shape culture

📖 References

  • Kotter, J. (1996/2012). Leading Change.
  • Schein, E. Organizational Culture and Leadership.
  • NIST (2023). AI Risk Management Framework 1.0.
  • ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — AI management systems.
  • Brynjolfsson, E., Rock, D. & Syverson, C. — The productivity J-curve.
  • European Union — Artificial Intelligence Act.

quiz.q: A CEO announces a new organisational structure to drive customer focus but leaves processes, incentives and performance measures unchanged. What is the MOST likely outcome?
opts: Rapid improvement in customer focus
Lower costs
Little change in behaviour, because the rest of the operating model still rewards old ways of working
Improved culture within three months
quiz.x: Structure alone rarely changes performance; operating-model elements must change together.

quiz.q: Six months into an AI-enabled process redesign, productivity has dropped 10%. The board wants to abandon it. What should the executive consider FIRST?
opts: Whether this is the expected J-curve dip, and whether learning and adoption indicators show progress toward recovery
Doubling the budget
Abandoning it immediately to stop losses
Replacing the project team
quiz.x: Major adoption often dips before improving. Leading indicators help distinguish a normal dip from failure.

quiz.q: Which AI use case is typically the STRONGEST early candidate for a business case?
opts: A broad initiative to 'make the whole company AI-first'
An AI system to make final hiring decisions without human review
Automated drafting of first-response emails for a high-volume service desk, with measurable time savings
Replacing the executive team's strategic decisions with AI
quiz.x: Narrow, high-volume, measurable use cases provide clear value with manageable risk; high-impact decisions require stronger oversight.

quiz.q: An HR team wants to deploy an AI system to screen job applicants. According to proportional AI governance, what is required?
opts: Approval from IT only
The same light controls as for internal meeting summaries
No controls if the vendor is reputable
Stronger controls: bias testing, human oversight, transparency and data protection, because it affects people's opportunities
quiz.x: Governance should match impact; hiring decisions are high-impact and many regulations treat them as high-risk.

quiz.q: A transformation leader announces victory after the first successful pilot, and the change team is disbanded. Which Kotter step is being neglected?
opts: Creating urgency
Sustaining acceleration and anchoring change rather than declaring victory too soon
Communicating the vision
Forming the vision
quiz.x: Early wins build momentum, but declaring victory early lets old habits return before change is embedded.

quiz.q: Executives say they want innovation but a manager who led a failed experiment is publicly demoted. What will the organisation MOST likely learn?
opts: That experimentation is risky and failure is punished, regardless of stated values
That only executives may innovate
That innovation is valued
That experiments must be larger
quiz.x: Culture is shaped by how leaders react and whom they reward or punish, not by stated values.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST describes the role of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?
opts: A tool for building AI models
A law that all organisations worldwide must follow
A certification for AI developers only
A voluntary framework structuring AI risk management around Govern, Map, Measure and Manage
quiz.x: NIST AI RMF is a voluntary framework; ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable management system standard; regulations like the EU AI Act are legal requirements.

quiz.q: A senior manager openly blocks a transformation the executive team has agreed. According to Kotter, what is the appropriate response?
opts: Ignore it and hope peer pressure works
Exclude the manager's unit from the transformation
Address the obstacle directly — coach, realign, or if necessary change who holds the role
Delay the transformation until the manager retires
quiz.x: Removing obstacles includes addressing leaders who resist; leaving them in place signals the change is optional.

quiz.q: An AI pilot is launched without defined success criteria. What is the MOST significant problem at the end of the pilot?
opts: The vendor will raise prices
There is no objective basis to decide whether to scale, adjust or stop
The team will be too large
Costs will be too high
quiz.x: Clear success criteria and a decision point make pilots useful for executive decisions.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of the 'personal role' section in the transformation charter?
opts: To commit the executive to what they will start, stop and model, since leader behaviour shapes whether change is real
To list the executive's achievements
To replace the change team
To assign blame for past failures
quiz.x: Executives lead transformation through visible personal behaviour; the charter makes that commitment explicit.

modules.d: Six executive coaching sessions turning the intensive into measurable results.
modules.body:
Why the 90 days matter more than the 3 days

Executive education produces insight; behaviour change happens afterwards, under pressure, in the real organisation. Without structured follow-through, most intensive learning fades within weeks as old routines reassert themselves. The 90-day coaching sprint exists to convert your transformation charter into results and your personal leadership commitments into habits.

How executive coaching works

Coaching is not consulting (giving answers) or therapy (healing the past). It is a disciplined conversation that helps you think more clearly, decide more deliberately and act more consistently. Sessions use the GROW model popularised by John Whitmore: Goal (what you want from this session and this quarter), Reality (what is actually happening, with evidence), Options (the range of possible actions), and Will (what you commit to do, by when, and how you will know). Good coaches ask more than they tell, challenge assumptions and hold you to your commitments.

The sprint structure

  • Session 1 (week 1–2) — Contracting and baseline. Confirm the charter, agree success measures for the 90 days, identify stakeholders who will observe your change, and set the coaching agreement: confidentiality, cadence, preparation expectations.
  • Session 2 (week 3–4) — First wins. Review progress on the first short-term wins; address early resistance; refine stakeholder engagement.
  • Session 3 (week 5–6) — Leadership behaviours. Focus on the personal behaviours you committed to change; review observer feedback using feedforward.
  • Session 4 (week 7–8) — Obstacles and decisions. Work through the hardest decision or relationship blocking progress — often a peer, a resistant leader or a resource trade-off.
  • Session 5 (week 9–10) — Sustaining and scaling. Plan how wins become embedded in processes, measures and promotions; prepare the leaders below you to carry the work.
  • Session 6 (week 11–12) — Review and sponsor debrief. Measure results against the baseline, gather observer feedback, capture lessons, and set the next 90-day agenda. A debrief with your sponsor closes the loop.
Preparation is the multiplier. Executives who arrive with a prepared update — progress on commitments, the issue they most need to think through, and evidence — get far more from each session than those who arrive to "see what comes up". Fifteen minutes of preparation is usually worth more than the session itself.

Stakeholder-centred measurement

Marshall Goldsmith's stakeholder-centred coaching measures change through the people who experience your leadership. You select a small group of stakeholders, tell them the behaviours you are working on, ask them for ongoing suggestions, and later ask them to rate whether you have become more or less effective. This creates both accountability and visible change — and it matters because leadership effectiveness is ultimately judged by others.

Measuring results, not activity

At the start of the sprint, define two kinds of measures. Organisational outcomes linked to your charter — for example, cycle time reduced, adoption rate of a new process, a strategic decision taken, an initiative stopped and resources redeployed. Leadership measures — observer ratings of your target behaviours, engagement indicators in your team, or the number of decisions delegated. Review both at sessions 3 and 6.

When progress stalls

Expect at least one stall. Common causes: overloaded calendars leaving no time for the charter, a key relationship blocking progress, or an unrealistic plan. The coaching response is not to push harder but to diagnose: Is this a priority problem (other things are winning), a capability problem (you or your team lack a skill), a relationship problem, or a design problem (the plan itself is wrong)? Each needs a different response.

After the sprint

Successful executives make the sprint rhythm permanent: a quarterly personal review of priorities and behaviours, continued stakeholder feedback, a coach or peer advisory group, and development of the leaders beneath them using the same tools. The goal is not to need the coach — it is to become a leader who coaches others.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my executive coach using the GROW model. Before we start, ask me for my transformation charter commitments and progress since our last session. Then run one coaching session: clarify my goal for today, probe the reality with evidence, help me generate options without giving me the answer, and end with specific commitments, deadlines and how I will measure them. Challenge me if I am avoiding the hardest issue.

📚 Glossary

  • GROW: Goal, Reality, Options, Will coaching model
  • Contracting: agreeing coaching goals, confidentiality and expectations
  • Stakeholder-centred coaching: measuring change through those who experience the leader's behaviour
  • Sponsor debrief: closing review with the executive's sponsor or board

📖 References

  • Whitmore, J. Coaching for Performance.
  • Goldsmith, M. — Stakeholder Centered Coaching.
  • International Coaching Federation — Core Competencies.
  • Watkins, M. (2013). The First 90 Days.

quiz.q: An executive asks their coach, 'Just tell me what to do about my underperforming COO.' What is the MOST appropriate coaching response?
opts: Use questions to clarify the goal, the facts about the COO's performance and the options, so the executive decides
Change the subject to a less sensitive topic
Refer the executive to HR
Give a specific recommendation, since the executive asked
quiz.x: Coaching helps the executive think and decide; giving answers turns it into consulting and reduces ownership.

quiz.q: An executive arrives at each session unprepared and says, 'Let's see what comes up.' Progress is slow. What would MOST improve results?
opts: Changing coaches
Extending each session
More frequent sessions
Preparing an update on commitments, the most important issue and evidence before each session
quiz.x: Preparation multiplies the value of each session.

quiz.q: Which measure BEST reflects stakeholder-centred coaching?
opts: The coach's assessment
Ratings from selected stakeholders on whether the executive has become more effective in the target behaviours
The number of coaching sessions attended
The executive's own rating of their improvement
quiz.x: Change is judged by those who experience the leader's behaviour.

quiz.q: At session 4, an executive has made no progress on the charter for three weeks because 'operations took all my time'. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
opts: A design problem
A capability problem
A priority problem — other demands are winning against the charter
A relationship problem
quiz.x: When time is consumed by other work, the issue is priority; the response is to restructure the calendar or delegate, not push harder.

quiz.q: Which commitment BEST reflects the 'Will' stage of GROW?
opts: I will think about the options
By Friday, I will meet each of my three direct reports to agree decision rights for the pricing project, and confirm in writing
I will try to improve communication with my team
Communication should improve
quiz.x: Will requires specific actions, deadlines and evidence of completion.

quiz.q: Why does session 1 set baseline measures?
opts: So results at session 6 can be compared objectively with the starting point
To satisfy HR requirements
To fill the session
To assess the coach
quiz.x: A baseline makes it possible to measure progress rather than rely on impressions.

quiz.q: An executive's charter progress is stalled because a peer division head refuses to share data. What type of problem is this, and what is a sensible coaching focus?
opts: A capability problem — attend a data course
A design problem — abandon the charter
A relationship problem — explore the peer's interests and options for influence
A priority problem — work longer hours
quiz.x: A blocking relationship calls for stakeholder understanding and influence strategies.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST distinguishes coaching from consulting?
opts: Coaching is only for underperforming leaders
Consultants focus on people, coaches on strategy
Coaches charge more than consultants
Coaches help leaders think, decide and act; consultants primarily provide expert answers and solutions
quiz.x: Coaching builds the leader's capability and ownership rather than supplying solutions.

quiz.q: At the end of the sprint, results are strong. What does the course recommend next?
opts: Repeat the same 90-day plan exactly
End all development activity
Make the rhythm permanent: quarterly reviews, continued feedback, and coaching others
Hand the charter to a consultant
quiz.x: Sustained growth comes from embedding the rhythm and developing others.

quiz.q: Why is confidentiality part of contracting in executive coaching?
opts: It allows the coach to avoid reporting
It is legally required in all countries
It prevents the sponsor from seeing results
It creates the trust needed for executives to discuss real problems honestly
quiz.x: Executives speak candidly only when they trust the conversation; results can still be shared through agreed measures and debriefs.
